d.title: T tokens give T−n+1 n-grams, and the probabilities are ratios of counts
d.caption: Six tokens yield 5 bigrams and 4 trigrams — **every extra word of context costs you one training example from the same sentence**, which is the first hint of the sparsity wall in §05. And the conditional probability is nothing more than a ratio: **`the` is followed by `cat` once and `mat` once, so each is 0.5 and the two sum to 1.** No parameters are estimated; the counts *are* the model.

d.title: One zero makes the whole sentence impossible
d.caption: `P(flew | cat)` is **0.0000** — not small, zero. And because the sentence probability is a **product** over positions, one unseen bigram sets the probability of the entire sentence to zero, however fluent the rest of it is. **So an unsmoothed model does not merely rank an unseen continuation last: it declares the sentence impossible**, which is why smoothing is not an optimisation but a requirement for the model to function at all.

steps.note: a product, so one zero wins

d.title: Add-one gives 61.5% of the mass to things never observed
d.caption: This is the cost stated as a number. **The MLE gives the seen continuations 1.000 of the probability mass; add-one leaves them 0.385** — so **61.5% of the distribution has been handed to events the corpus never saw**, simply because the vocabulary is 10 and the context count is 3. The denominator `count(c) + |V|` is the whole problem: **the correction scales with the vocabulary, not with the evidence**, so a realistic `|V|` makes it worse, not better.

d.title: Perplexity is a branching factor, and it is only comparable within a tokenization
d.caption: **4.93 on training against 6.58 held out, where uniform guessing over this 10-word vocabulary would be 10** — so the model is doing real work and doing less of it on unseen text, which is the gap you watch. The published figures tell the field's story: **a trigram narrows the next word to about 80 candidates and GPT-4 to under 10.** But they are only comparable across models sharing a vocabulary and tokenization — **a larger vocabulary faces a harder prediction, so its number is not a worse model.**

d.title: Each extra word of context multiplies the table by 50,000
d.caption: **A 3-gram table over a 50,000-word vocabulary has 1.25×10¹⁴ cells and a 4-gram table 6.25×10¹⁸** — more cells than there are words in any corpus, so **the overwhelming majority of entries are zero and the model is mostly smoothing.** And three other limits are structural rather than about size: **a fixed context window cannot see a verb agreeing with a subject six words back, and `good` and `great` stay unrelated symbols, so seeing one teaches nothing about the other.**

d.title: A claim about text alone, which is exactly why it scales
d.caption: Firth's line from 1957 is the whole basis of the field. **If two words appear in the same contexts — *the ___ ran across the garden* — then whatever they mean, they mean something similar enough to be substitutable there.** And note what the claim does **not** require: no dictionary, no labels, no linguistics, no annotation budget. **Every method in this lesson is a different way of turning co-occurrence counts into vectors, and all of them rest on this one assumption.**

nodes.label: No dictionary, no labels, no linguistics
Which is why it scales
nodes.sub: more text is the only input

nodes.label: Every method here rests on it

d.title: Fifty thousand dot products per pair, replaced by K+1
d.caption: The honest objective is a softmax over **every** word in the vocabulary — 50,000 dot products and a normalisation, **for every training pair, of which there are billions.** Negative sampling asks a cheaper question: **push the true context word's score up and `K` randomly sampled words' scores down, with `K` typically 5 to 20.** The samples come from the unigram distribution raised to **0.75**, which flattens it — **an empirical exponent rather than a principled one**, chosen to stop common words dominating the negatives while still sampling them more often than rare ones.

d.title: Six groups, the same gap in every one, and no labels anywhere
d.caption: **Within-group cosine near 0.99 and across-group well under 0.45, in all six groups** — from 4,000 sentences, 63,736 pairs, six epochs and **no labels at all.** The gap is the structure the model found from co-occurrence alone. And the comparison that makes it mean something: **with one-hot, the cosine between any two distinct words is exactly 0.000, so there is no gap because there is no structure** — and nothing a downstream model could generalise from.

d.title: Three methods, and only one of them survives an unseen word
d.caption: Word2Vec and GloVe differ in **where the counts come from** — sampled local windows against the corpus-wide co-occurrence matrix, factorised directly — and they share the same hard limit: **a word absent from training has no vector, so there is nothing to look up.** FastText changes the unit: **a word's vector is the sum of its character n-gram vectors**, so an unseen word is still built from pieces that were seen. Which is 1.3's subword argument arriving in the embedding layer.

d.title: The result is real and the demonstration is stage-managed
d.caption: The analogy works when a relation happens to be a consistent **translation** in the vector space, and for some relations it genuinely is — a real and surprising property of embeddings trained on enough text. **But the standard evaluation excludes the three input words from the candidate answers, and without that exclusion the nearest vector to `king − man + woman` is frequently `king` itself.** Worth knowing both halves, **because the analogy is often cited as evidence that embeddings capture meaning more strongly than the geometry supports.**

nodes.label: Without that, the answer is often 'king'
So: the result holds, the demo is staged
It is cited as more than it shows

d.title: Five spans, five labels, and one distinction people collapse
d.caption: NER finds **spans** and labels them — note that `Apple Inc.` is two tokens and one entity, which is what §02 is about. The label set is `PERSON, ORG, GPE, LOC, DATE, TIME, MONEY, PERCENT, PRODUCT, EVENT, WORK_OF_ART, LAW, LANGUAGE`, and **`GPE` and `LOC` are genuinely distinct: a country is a political entity, a mountain range is not.** Collapsing them is a modelling decision, not a tidy-up — and it is usually made by accident.

d.title: Two adjacent people, and the scheme decides whether they are one person
d.caption: This is why the `B-` exists, and it takes one example to show: **`IO` decodes `Steve Jobs Tim Cook` to ONE span of four tokens; `BIO` decodes it to two.** Without a begin tag there is no way to express a boundary between two adjacent entities of the same type. **BIOES** makes every boundary explicit rather than inferred, at `4n+1` tags instead of `2n+1` — **73 classes instead of 37 at 18 entity types**, which is the cost to weigh against a usually-small gain.

d.title: 83.3% token accuracy and 0.50 span F1, on the same prediction
d.caption: One token wrong — the third `I-PER` predicted as `O` — and the two metrics describe different worlds. **Token accuracy says 83.3% because five of six tags are right. Span F1 says 0.50, because the PER span is now `(0,1)` instead of `(0,2)`, and a span that is nearly right is wrong.** Which is the correct way to score it: **a downstream system extracts the span, so a truncated name is a wrong name, not an 83%-right one.**

d.title: Six of twenty-five transitions are structurally impossible
d.caption: `O` to `I-PER` is not a mistake the model should be slightly discouraged from — **it is not a valid tag sequence at all**, because an inside tag with no begin before it decodes to nothing. **A per-token classifier can emit it, because it scores each position independently; a CRF scores the sequence, so it can learn a transition weight that makes the invalid moves unreachable.** That is the whole contribution: **6 of 25 transitions here are structurally invalid, and only a sequence model can rule them out.**

state: a per-token model can emit them

d.title: Five approaches, and the production answer is two of them at once
d.caption: **A regex is exact, auditable and free, and no learned model will beat it on a pattern that is genuinely a pattern** — postcodes, order numbers, ISINs, dates in a known format. Transformers are the accuracy ceiling for the open categories, because people, organisations and products need context. **LLM zero-shot is for the long tail: a new entity type tomorrow with no labelled data, at a cost per document and with output that varies between calls.** Hence the last row: **rules for the formatted entities, a model for the open ones, and a merge step where rules win.**

d.title: The same word, two tags, decided by the sentence
d.caption: `book`, `play` and `duck` each take two different tags in two different sentences — **so a part-of-speech tag is not a property of a word, it is a property of a word in a position**, and a lookup table cannot produce it. That is also the cleanest statement of what 1.4's representations were missing. Two tag sets exist for a reason: **`pos_` is 17 coarse universal tags designed to be comparable across languages, and `tag_` is the finer Penn Treebank set** that distinguishes `VBZ` from `VBP`.

steps.code: 'The duck can fly' / 'I duck under it'

d.title: Twelve tokens between the subject and its verb
d.caption: Two sentences with **identical bags of words** get opposite triples from the parse — `(cat, chased, mouse)` against `(mouse, chased, cat)` — which is the structure 1.4's representation discarded. And the second measurement is the one that sets up module 4: in *“The engineers who joined the company last year from several different teams were promoted”*, **the subject and its verb are 12 tokens apart, and the agreement spans that whole distance. A bigram model sees only `(teams, were)` and has no way to know.**

d.title: Three phrases, each with its head and its grammatical role attached
d.caption: **A noun chunk is a noun plus the words describing it, read straight off the parse — the cheapest useful phrase extractor there is.** *machine learning engineers* comes out as **one unit rather than three tokens**, with `root=engineers` and `dep=nsubj`, so you get the phrase and what it is doing in the sentence in one pass. For key-phrase extraction, building a knowledge graph, or turning a sentence into a triple, **that pairing is the part that saves work.**
